subtitle: How a potter’s blade carried Sushruta’s shadow to London

panels.shot: dramatic mid-shot, split composition with Pune on one side and Georgian London on the other
panels.action: Cowasjee and the Pune Surgeon stand back to back, the Surgeon holding a small leaf-shaped blade, while beyond them rise the tiled roofs of Pune on one side and the smoky skyline of London on the other.

dialogue.text: In 1793, on a dusty road near Pune, a potter-surgeon rebuilt Cowasjee’s nose—and the news crossed oceans to remake surgery in London.

i18n.hi: १७९३ में, पुणे के पास धूल भरी राह पर, एक कुम्हार-हकीम ने कावसजी की नाक फिर बना दी — और ये ख़बर सागर पार कर लंदन की सर्जरी बदल गई।

panels.shot: wide shot of battlefield aftermath, low angle with distant fort
panels.action: Cowasjee, his face partly in shadow, walks among defeated soldiers and broken standards near a Deccan fort, his posture stooped with shame as he hides his mutilated face in his shawl.

dialogue.text: In the wars of late eighteenth-century India, punishment could mark a body for life. Many defeated soldiers had their noses cut to break their honour.

i18n.hi: अठारहवीं सदी के आख़िरी हिंदुस्तानी युद्धों में सज़ा देह पर उम्र भर के लिए लिखी जाती थी। हारे सिपाहियों की नाकें काट दी जातीं, उनकी इज़्ज़त मिटाने को।

panels.shot: medium close-up on Cowasjee, three-quarter profile
panels.action: Cowasjee sits alone under a tree on the outskirts of Pune, his head bowed, the central part of his nose missing, eyes hollow and distant as travellers pass by without meeting his gaze.

dialogue.speaker: Cowasjee and the Pune Surgeon
dialogue.text: How does a man walk in the bazaar without a face?

i18n.hi: बाज़ार में कोई चेहरा बिना आदमी कैसे चले?

panels.shot: busy street-level shot in Pune bazaar, slightly above eye level
panels.action: In a crowded Pune lane of shops and bullock-carts, Cowasjee keeps to the side while a middle-aged artisan, the Pune Surgeon, examines a clay pot with practiced fingers, his tools hanging in a cloth bundle at his waist.

dialogue.text: Near Pune lived a man whom British observers called a Kumhar—a potter by caste, a surgeon by practice. In his hands, clay and flesh both obeyed the same steady eye.

i18n.hi: पुणे के पास वही आदमी रहता था, जिसे अंग्रेज़ नज़रें कुम्हार कहती थीं — जाति से कुम्हार, काम से सर्जन। उसकी उँगलियों में मिट्टी और माँस दोनों उसी ठहरती नज़र से झुक जाते।

panels.shot: intimate mid-shot inside a modest courtyard, soft side lighting
panels.action: In a shaded courtyard with a worn stone floor, the Pune Surgeon calmly studies Cowasjee’s mutilated nose, gently lifting his chin while family members watch anxiously from the doorway.

dialogue.speaker: Cowasjee and the Pune Surgeon
dialogue.text: If you can do this, ustad, I will bear any pain.

i18n.hi: उस्ताद, आप ये कर दें, तो मैं हर दर्द सह लूँगा।

panels.shot: close-up on the Pune Surgeon’s hands and tools, top-down view
panels.action: On a low wooden board, the Pune Surgeon lays out his simple instruments—a leaf-shaped knife, small forceps, strips of cloth, and a flat metal plate—while a brass oil lamp casts sharp shadows.

dialogue.text: His method echoed verses of the old Sushruta Samhita, yet no scholar can trace the thread. The craft had survived not in palm-leaf libraries, but in working hands.

i18n.hi: उसकी कारीगरी में पुराने सुश्रुत संहिता की धुन गूँजती थी, पर कोई पंडित उस डोर को पकड़ नहीं पाता। ये हुनर ताड़-पत्रों में नहीं, काम करती हथेलियों में बचा रहा।

panels.shot: tight close-up on Cowasjee’s forehead, surgeon’s hand marking outlines
panels.action: The Pune Surgeon, brow furrowed in concentration, lightly traces a pattern on Cowasjee’s forehead with a red-tinted twig, outlining a leaf-shaped flap while Cowasjee grips the edge of the stool.

dialogue.text: He marked a flap on the forehead, shaped like a leaf. The skin would stay tethered above, a living bridge to feed the new nose.

i18n.hi: उसने माथे पर पत्ती जैसी एक खाल की पट्टी खींची। खाल ऊपर से जुड़ी रही — नयी नाक को खून देने वाला एक ज़िंदा पुल।

panels.shot: dramatic side profile of both men, mid-shot, tight focus
panels.action: Cowasjee reclines as the Pune Surgeon leans in with his blade, his face composed and precise; behind them a helper holds a simple cloth band ready, the courtyard still in tense silence.

dialogue.text: Under the open sky, without ether or chloroform, he cut and turned the flap down, stitching it to the ruined nose with fine thread and quiet confidence.

i18n.hi: खुले आसमान तले, बिना ईथर या क्लोरोफॉर्म, उसने पट्टी काटकर नीचे पलट दी, और महीन सूत व चुप्प सुकून से उसे टूटी नाक पर टाँक दिया।

panels.shot: medium shot showing bandaged face, with surgeon adjusting dressings
panels.action: With Cowasjee’s face swathed in cloth that binds his forehead to his nose, the Pune Surgeon gently adjusts the bandage, his hands steady while a clay pot of herbal paste sits nearby.

dialogue.text: He smeared herbal pastes, secured the flap, and left a small tube to keep the nostrils open. Days turned into weeks as skin learned its new shape.

i18n.hi: उसने जड़ी-बूटी का लेप लगाया, पट्टी कसी, और नथुनों को खुला रखने को एक नली छोड़ दी। दिन हफ़्तों में बदले, खाल ने नया ढाँचा सीख लिया।

panels.shot: mirror-like frontal shot, Cowasjee looking at reflection in metal plate
panels.action: Cowasjee stares into a polished metal plate held by the Pune Surgeon, his eyes widening as he sees the outline of a new nose on his face, the skin slightly swollen but whole.

dialogue.speaker: Cowasjee and the Pune Surgeon
dialogue.text: It is mine… and yet it is borrowed from my own brow.

i18n.hi: ये मेरी है… फिर भी मेरे ही माथे से उधार ली गई है।

panels.shot: wide shot in a British East India Company camp tent, interior
panels.action: Inside a canvas tent flying the Company flag, two British officers, representing Thomas Cruso and James Findlay, lean forward in curiosity as the Pune Surgeon, calm and barefoot, stands beside Cowasjee, who sits with his healing nose.

dialogue.text: Two British surgeons in Company service, Thomas Cruso and James Findlay, saw the result. A living nose, fashioned from forehead skin, where a mutilated scar had been.

i18n.hi: कंपनी के दो अंग्रेज़ सर्जन, थॉमस क्रूसो और जेम्स फ़ाइंडले, ने नतीजा देखा — माथे की खाल से गढ़ी ज़िंदा नाक, जहाँ पहले एक कटी हुई दाग़ थी।

panels.shot: close-up on Cowasjee’s face and a British observer sketching in the background
panels.action: Cruso, seated at a small desk, carefully sketches Cowasjee’s profile in a notebook, while Cowasjee sits patiently, his new nose in clear profile and the Pune Surgeon watching from the side.

dialogue.speaker: Cowasjee and the Pune Surgeon
dialogue.text: You wish to carry this drawing to your people?

i18n.hi: तुम ये नक़्शा अपने लोगों तक ले जाना चाहते हो?

panels.shot: bird’s-eye view of a London study cluttered with papers, candlelight
panels.action: Years later, in a London study lit by candles, a gentleman reads aloud from a manuscript while an engraver copies a drawing of the Indian method, showing the forehead flap swung down to the nose.

dialogue.text: In October 1794, the Gentleman’s Magazine printed their account. In London, readers studied the engraving of an Indian rhinoplasty with a forehead flap, intrigued and skeptical.

i18n.hi: अक्टूबर १७९४ में, जेंटलमैन’ज़ मैगज़ीन ने उनकी रिपोर्ट छापी। लंदन में लोगों ने माथे की खाल से बनी हिंदुस्तानी नाक की नक़्क़ाशी देखी — हैरत से, शक से।

panels.shot: medium shot of Joseph Carpue in an anatomical theatre, slight low angle
panels.action: In an early nineteenth-century anatomical theatre, Joseph Carpue stands before a chalkboard sketch of the Indian method, addressing a small group of attentive students seated on wooden benches.

dialogue.text: Joseph Constantine Carpue studied these reports. Europe knew surgery, but not this. After careful trials, he resolved to try the Indian method in London.

i18n.hi: जोसेफ़ कॉन्स्टैन्टाइन कारप्यू ने ये बयान पढ़े। यूरोप को सर्जरी आती थी, पर ये नहीं। कड़े अभ्यासों के बाद उसने तय किया कि लंदन में यही हिंदुस्तानी तरीका आज़माएगा।

panels.shot: mid-shot of Carpue operating, echoing the Pune scene, cross-cut composition
panels.action: Carpue leans over a patient in a London operating room, lifting a forehead flap with his knife, while in a ghosted overlay behind him, the Pune Surgeon is seen in the same pose in his courtyard years earlier.

dialogue.text: In 1814, he performed his first such operation, then another. In 1816, he published their stories, tracing his technique to the Indian forehead flap he had read about.

i18n.hi: १८१४ में उसने पहली ऐसी सर्जरी की, फिर दूसरी। १८१६ में उसने उनकी कहानियाँ छापीं, और अपनी तकनीक की रेखा उस हिंदुस्तानी माथे की पट्टी तक पहुँचाई, जिसके बारे में वो पढ़ चुका था।

panels.shot: montage wide shot, timeline-like, spanning India and Europe
panels.action: A sweeping panel shows, from left to right, Sushruta teaching students under a tree, the Pune Surgeon operating on Cowasjee, and Carpue lecturing in London, each linked by a faint flowing line.

dialogue.text: Modern scholars see the resemblance to Sushruta’s ancient verses, but the path is broken. Between Sanskrit text and London theatre stand nameless healers, artisans, and patients like Cowasjee.

i18n.hi: आज के विद्वानों को इसमें सुश्रुत की पुरानी पंक्तियों की छाया दिखती है, पर राह कहीं टूटी है। संस्कृत ग्रंथ से लंदन के थियेटर के बीच अनगिनत बेनाम वैद्य, कारीगर और कावसजी जैसे मरीज़ खड़े हैं।

panels.shot: introspective close-up on the Pune Surgeon in his courtyard at dusk
panels.action: At dusk in his modest courtyard, the Pune Surgeon washes his hands at a small stone basin, his face tired yet content, while Cowasjee, in the background, walks through the gate with his head held high.

dialogue.text: The Gentleman’s Magazine named the Kumhar, not as a vaidya, but as a potter. His caste rank stayed low, even as his method climbed into European books.

i18n.hi: जेंटलमैन’ज़ मैगज़ीन ने उस कुम्हार का नाम वैद्य नहीं, कुम्हार ही लिखा। उसकी जाति नीचे रही, जबकि उसका हुनर यूरोपीय किताबों की ऊँचाइयों पर चढ़ गया।

panels.shot: final contemplative wide shot, present-day hospital corridor dissolving from old courtyard
panels.action: A present-day hospital corridor in soft focus seems to emerge from the old Pune courtyard, with a modern surgeon walking past, while faintly above, the figures of Cowasjee and the Pune Surgeon look on.

dialogue.text: Cowasjee’s rebuilt nose shows how knowledge can outlive the status of its makers—travelling from a potter’s yard in Pune to shape the very face of modern plastic surgery.

i18n.hi: कावसजी की नयी नाक दिखाती है कि ज्ञान अपने बनाने वालों की हैसियत से आगे निकल जाता है — पुणे की कुम्हार-ड्यारी से उठकर आधुनिक प्लास्टिक सर्जरी के चेहरे को गढ़ने तक।

subtitle_i18n.en: How a potter’s blade carried Sushruta’s shadow to London
subtitle_i18n.hi: कैसे एक कुम्हार की छुरी ने सुश्रुत की परछाईं लंदन तक पहुँचा दी
